title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) to measure the marginal benefit of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and produced one shared generator output per task (shared_initial_generation). Requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0). We release full preregistration and execution artifacts (preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5c..., raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce925...) and interpret the null outcome as a ceiling case specific to this task/model/validator regime. We discuss design implications for future verifier‑utility evaluations and provide exact replay provenance.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation promises operational speedups in NetOps but risks outages if generated changes violate ordering/dependency constraints. A common mitigation is the generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pattern: an LLM proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks safety and policy constraints, and an automated repair step attempts to fix violations before application. Prior work and proposals argue for such pipelines, but quantitative estimates of marginal verifier value—when measured under strict, preregistered conditions—are rare. We preregistered a paired confirmatory protocol (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) to quantify the marginal change in regression‑causing change rate when a deterministic verifier+repair layer is inserted. The design holds the generator output fixed across arms (shared_initial_generation) so that any difference in binary validator outcome can be attributed to the verifier/repair intervention alone. Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing G→V→R against LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks; (2) complete, cryptographically hashed artifact release for exact replay (key hashes below); (3) a transparent null result (ceiling case) together with design guidance for future evaluations that seek to demonstrate verifier/repair utility in failure‑rich operational regimes.
sections.related_work: LLM assistance for NetOps and AIOps spans intent translation, configuration synthesis, and closed‑loop agentic workflows that use verification and repair. Benchmarks and pipelines that combine generation with formal or emulation‑based verification (generate→validate→repair) report that verifier guidance can reduce regressions when generator error is nontrivial (see Cornetto and related generate‑validate‑repair research). Position papers argue for confining LLMs to translation tasks while relying on deterministic solvers for long‑horizon reasoning; others explore evolving/verifier‑assisted verifiers or hybrid tool‑orchestrated agents for operational safety. Our experiment differs methodologically: by preregistering a paired design that fixes the generator output and archives verifier traces, we isolate the marginal verifier effect and publish the full provenance so others can replay and extend the analysis. Representative prior leads used to motivate coverage, validator design, and task synthesis are cited in the evidence bundle (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory framing. The full preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) was frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622). Primary hypothesis H1: the G→V→R pipeline yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than LLM‑only (estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Power assumptions (target baseline failure = 0.20 and target absolute reduction = 0.08) were preregistered and are reported explicitly in the archive; sensitivity scans were included but remain secondary to the confirmatory test.
Task pool, deterministic sampling, and inclusion rules. Tasks were generated by a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and filtered to intents covered by the preregistered validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). To avoid human selection bias we deterministically selected K=200 tasks by computing SHA‑256(intent_string), sorting ascending, and taking the first K after automated coverage filtering. All selection, filtering, and exclusion decisions were logged and archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256: f1d447b7...). The task manifest contains per‑task payloads: initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow constraints, required_sequence, and difficulty metadata (examples are included in the representative_tasks archive).
Paired shared_initial_generation design. For each task we made a single generator call (shared_initial_generation) that produced candidate configuration c. The baseline arm treated c as the suggestion; the guarded arm first ran the deterministic validator on c and, only if the validator flagged violations, was a single preregistered repair call permitted (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This pairing isolates verifier marginal effect by holding the generator output identical across arms. The execution contract and budget: maximum_model_calls = 400 (planned 1 generator call per task); actual model_calls_used = 200 because one shared generator call covered both arms per task. Model and provider configuration are archived (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...). Requested_model = gpt-5-mini; adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1.
Validator, scoring, and repair semantics. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) parses generated text into structured commands and enforces preregistered workflow and dependency checks (examples: shutdown before MTU change; minimum‑up constraints across interface groups; protected interface invariants). Scoring is binary (valid==true means candidate satisfies all preregistered constraints). When valid==false, the repair policy permitted a single constrained repair invocation; repair attempts and repair_applied flags were logged. All scoring traces were archived under execution/scoring/*.json for replay (representative files and hashes are listed in the execution manifest). The scorer version used was v5.0 and all per‑episode validator final_state snapshots, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and violation codes are preserved for audit.
Statistical analysis plan. The preregistered primary test is the two‑sided exact McNemar test on the paired binary outcome (validator pass/fail). We computed the paired contingency table n11,n10,n01,n00 and used a paired bootstrap percentile interval (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) to produce a 95% CI for the paired difference. Secondary estimands (time to deploy, model calls per successful apply) were preregistered but became moot because no repairs were invoked; nevertheless their logs and calculation scripts were archived in analysis/. All analysis code, seeds, and outputs are archived with SHA‑256 checksums (analysis/*).

sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling case and its meaning. The observed null result is a degenerate but informative ceiling case: within the sampled deterministic task pool, for the requested_model (gpt-5-mini) and the deterministic validator used, generated candidates satisfied all preregistered constraints; therefore the verifier never had an opportunity to change the binary apply outcome and the repair pathway was unused. This does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in production; rather it documents a regime where the generator+task distribution align with verifier coverage and produce validator‑compliant outputs.
Design implications for future confirmatory evaluations. To demonstrate verifier/repair usefulness in a confirmatory framework one must sample failure‑rich regimes. Practical design adjustments (all consistent with our archived artifacts and analysis): (1) increase baseline error propensity by sampling near validator boundaries or by including historical production failure cases; (2) evaluate weaker or multiple generator models to produce a nonzero baseline error rate; (3) include intentionally perturbed generator outputs (adversarial or noisy variants) that force verifier engagement; (4) change estimand to measure generator adaptation by allowing an interactive generator–verifier loop where generator receives verifier feedback and can produce repaired candidates—this moves away from shared_initial_generation but captures real agentic workflows where verifier feedback drives generation.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: preserved via deterministic sampling, seed logging, and cryptographic hashing of all artifacts; the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation confirm internal accounting. Construct validity: depends on how well deterministic_netops_validator_v5 models operationally meaningful regressions—our results are only as informative as the validator’s fidelity. External validity: limited by single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and coverage filtering to validator‑covered intents. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline=0.20) were violated because observed baseline=1.0; in such mismatched conditions the original power calculation is not informative and exact tests plus bootstrap intervals are the appropriate summaries (we report both). All these points and their evidence traces are archived and hashed in execution/ and analysis/.
Operational implications for practitioners. Operators should not infer that verifiers are redundant from this run. Instead, the artifact bundle provides a reproducible recipe to test whether verifiers add value in a target environment: (i) assemble a task pool rich in historical failures or boundary cases; (ii) run the paired shared_initial_generation design to isolate marginal verifier effect, or run interactive generator–verifier designs to measure adaptive benefits; (iii) use deterministic validators with auditable traces and record per‑change final_state snapshots for postmortem analysis. Our archived traces provide a concrete example and starting point for such evaluations.
Reproducibility and reuse. All code, inputs, outputs, and hashes required to reproduce the run are archived. Key entry points: preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5c..., raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 1acce925..., and master prompt provenance file provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e.... The execution_manifest enumerates per‑file SHA‑256 hashes and paths (execution/execution_manifest.json). To replay: (1) obtain the deterministic task generator and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 f1d447b7...); (2) for each task, replay the shared_initial_provider_call trace and the validator scoring trace under deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (3) rerun the paired analysis using the archived analysis scripts and seeds (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing generate→verify→repair to an LLM‑only acceptance policy on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks. Under the sampled task/model/validator regime the verifier produced no marginal benefit: both arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked. This ceiling case highlights a critical experimental design point: to measure verifier utility, one must evaluate on distributions where baseline generator errors are nontrivial or explicitly sample verifier boundary cases. We publish the full preregistration and exhaustive artifact bundle (with SHA‑256 hashes) so that future work can replay, extend, and design failure‑rich confirmatory evaluations that more directly probe operational verifier value.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect (baseline success = 100%) eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable training overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged items for this run.
